prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LAHORE, Pakistan (CNN) -- Two Pakistani television networks that transmit from Dubai in United Arab Emirates were ordered off the air Friday at the request of Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf, officials from the networks said. Pakistan's president, Gen. Pervez Musharraf, has been under pressure to lift a state of emergency. GEO-TV and ARY Digital offer a variety of programming, including news, entertainment, sports and music. Both networks had been banned from Pakistan's cable television system -- along with other networks, including CNN and BBC -- since Musharraf declared a state of emergency on November 3. This latest action prevents the two Pakistani networks from broadcasting worldwide via satellite. "This was basically our window to the world, GEO President Imran Aslan said. "In Pakistan, we've been shut down since the 3rd." The action was not wholly unexpected, but surprising nevertheless, Aslan said. "We uplink from Dubai, never having had a license to uplink from Pakistan," he said. "Dubai is a media city which seemed to be a haven and a sanctuary." Aslan said network officials have been in discussions with Pakistani government officials and "it seemed very obvious that they were going to do this. We were ready for it to a certain extent." "Eventually they decided to put their feet on the pipe, as it were." The government has made numerous demands of the network, although none of them official, Aslan said. "It's done through intermediaries," he said. "[Dulling] down the content, not having certain anchors, some of the hosts of our programs and talk shows." Musharraf's emergency order put several restrictions on the media, preventing journalists from expressing opinions prejudicial to "the ideology ... or integrity of Pakistan." Journalists are also restricted from covering suicide bombings and militant activity and could face three-year jail terms if they "ridicule" members of the government or armed forces. Almost a dozen journalists have been arrested. Musharraf has denied that his restrictions bar criticism, saying they only ask for responsibility in reporting. But last week, Pakistan expelled three print journalists for using language in an editorial that a Pakistani official called offensive to Musharraf. The editorial criticized Musharraf and the United States and Britain for continuing to support him. While many Pakistani journalists have protested the restrictions, some smaller television channels have complied with the government's restrictions. GEO and ARY have refused. "It seems most of the other channels have kowtowed in order to survive," Aslan said. Musharraf has said the emergency order improves stability and will foster peaceful parliamentary elections, which he has said he would like to see take place before January 9. The exact date will be set by Pakistan's Election Commission. Opposition leaders have accused Musharraf of declaring emergency rule to keep his hold on power and avoid an expected court ruling that would have nullified his election victory in October. Musharraf has been under pressure to lift the state of emergency.

“It’s done through intermediaries,” he said. “[Dulling] down the content, not having certain anchors, some of the hosts of our programs and talk shows.”

Musharraf’s emergency order imposed several restrictions on the media, preventing journalists from expressing opinions prejudicial to “the ideology … or integrity of Pakistan.”

Journalists are also restricted from covering suicide bombings and militant activity and could face three-year prison terms if they “ridicule” members of the government or armed forces. Almost a dozen journalists have been arrested.

Musharraf has denied that the restrictions prohibit criticism, saying they merely call for responsible reporting.

LAHORE, Pakistan (CNN) — Officials at two Pakistani TV companies said Friday that authorities in the United Arab Emirates had halted their Dubai-based transmissions following a request from Pakistani President Gen. Pervez Musharraf.

Musharraf was facing growing demands to end the state of emergency he imposed on November 3. Since that declaration, GEO-TV and ARY Digital—networks carrying news, sports, entertainment, and music—had already been removed from cable systems inside Pakistan. CNN, the BBC, and several other broadcasters were also blocked.

The new measure stopped GEO and ARY from distributing their programming by satellite to viewers around the world.

GEO President Imran Aslan described the Dubai transmission as the network’s only international outlet, noting that GEO had been unable to operate in Pakistan since November 3. Although company officials had anticipated the possibility of a shutdown, he said the decision was still startling.

Aslan explained that GEO had always sent its signal from Dubai because it never possessed authorization to uplink from Pakistan. Dubai’s media district, he said, had appeared to offer a secure refuge for broadcasters.

According to Aslan, GEO representatives had been speaking with Pakistani officials, and it had become increasingly clear that the government intended to take such action. The network had therefore prepared to some degree. He characterized the final move as the authorities effectively cutting off the flow altogether.

He also said the government had communicated several unofficial demands through intermediaries. Those requests included softening GEO’s coverage and removing particular news anchors, talk-show presenters, and other program hosts.

Restrictions introduced under Musharraf’s emergency decree barred media workers from voicing views considered harmful to Pakistan’s ideology or territorial integrity. Reporters were also limited in how they could cover militant operations and suicide attacks. Anyone found to have mocked members of the government or military could receive a prison sentence of up to three years. Nearly 12 journalists had been detained.

Musharraf rejected claims that the rules prohibited criticism, arguing instead that they merely required the media to report responsibly.

The previous week, however, Pakistan expelled three newspaper journalists over wording in an editorial that one Pakistani official said was insulting to Musharraf. The piece condemned Musharraf and also criticized the United States and Britain for maintaining their support for him.

Many journalists in Pakistan protested the media controls. Some smaller television stations accepted the government’s conditions, but GEO and ARY refused to do so. Aslan said most competing channels appeared to have submitted to the authorities in order to remain in operation.

Musharraf maintained that emergency rule would strengthen stability and help ensure peaceful parliamentary voting. He said he wanted the elections held before January 9, although Pakistan’s Election Commission was responsible for choosing the precise date.

Opposition figures argued that Musharraf imposed the emergency to preserve his grip on office and prevent an anticipated court decision from invalidating his October election victory.

## Musharraf Government Forces Geo and ARY News Off Air as Media Crackdown Deepens

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan — November 2007** — President Gen. Pervez Musharraf’s government has forced Pakistan’s two largest private television networks, Geo TV and ARY Digital, off the air as authorities intensify restrictions on independent media during the state of emergency imposed earlier this month.

Geo News and ARY One World, the networks’ news channels, disappeared from cable systems across Pakistan soon after Musharraf suspended the Constitution and declared emergency rule on November 3. The broadcasters initially continued transmitting by satellite from Dubai, but those broadcasts were also halted after pressure from Pakistani authorities and intervention by officials in the United Arab Emirates.

The shutdown left millions of Pakistanis without access to the country’s most influential private news services at a moment of acute political crisis. State-run Pakistan Television remained on air, while several private entertainment and sports channels continued operating.

Officials said the restrictions were necessary to prevent inflammatory reporting and protect national stability. Journalists and opposition politicians described the measures as censorship intended to suppress coverage of protests, arrests and challenges to Musharraf’s continued rule.

### New restrictions on broadcasters

Soon after proclaiming the emergency, Musharraf’s administration amended regulations governing electronic media and imposed a strict code of conduct on broadcasters. The measures prohibited or sharply limited live coverage of demonstrations, statements by political opponents and material deemed to ridicule the president, the armed forces or state institutions.

The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority, known as PEMRA, was given expanded powers to suspend licenses, seize equipment and close broadcasting facilities. Cable operators were ordered to remove channels that did not comply.

Authorities also restricted images of police confronting protesters and warned broadcasters against airing commentary about judges who opposed the emergency. Talk shows featuring opposition leaders, lawyers and independent analysts were suspended or heavily constrained.

Geo and ARY were among the outlets most affected because of their extensive live coverage of the political turmoil and their popular current-affairs programs. Both networks had closely followed the confrontation between Musharraf and the judiciary, including the struggle surrounding Chief Justice Iftikhar Muhammad Chaudhry.

### Broadcasts from Dubai halted

After being blocked inside Pakistan, Geo and ARY continued attempting to reach viewers through satellite transmissions originating in Dubai Media City. Within days, however, those news broadcasts were also taken off the air.

Executives at the networks said they had been ordered to stop broadcasting news from Dubai. The interruption demonstrated the Pakistani government’s ability to exert pressure beyond its borders and further narrowed the information available to viewers at home.

Geo officials said the network would not accept conditions that undermined editorial independence. The company warned that the shutdown threatened thousands of jobs and inflicted serious financial losses. ARY representatives likewise protested the suspension of their news operations, although portions of the network’s entertainment programming remained available.

Some services were later permitted to resume under restrictions, but the main news channels remained under intense government pressure.

### Journalists condemn censorship

Pakistani journalists responded with demonstrations, black armbands and symbolic news blackouts. Reporters, editors and camera crews gathered outside press clubs in Islamabad, Karachi, Lahore and other cities to demand the restoration of suspended channels and the repeal of the emergency media regulations.

The Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists and other media organizations said the government was attempting to reverse the expansion of independent broadcasting that had taken place earlier in Musharraf’s rule. Police detained or confronted some journalists covering protests, while media workers reported harassment and threats.

Journalists argued that the crackdown was particularly dangerous because it came during a constitutional crisis in which independent scrutiny was essential. Some television presenters moved discussions to alternative platforms, while viewers turned to foreign satellite channels, radio, newspapers and the internet for information.

International press-freedom organizations also criticized the closures. They said the regulations were broadly worded and allowed the government to punish legitimate reporting under the pretext of protecting national security.

### Emergency follows confrontation with judiciary

The media restrictions formed part of a broader campaign launched after Musharraf declared emergency rule. The president suspended constitutional guarantees, dismissed or detained judges, restricted political activity and ordered the arrest of lawyers, human-rights activists and opposition figures.

Musharraf said Pakistan faced threats from terrorism, judicial interference and political instability. His critics said the emergency was designed primarily to preserve his authority as the Supreme Court considered challenges to his October re-election as president while he remained army chief.

Private television had played a central role in the months leading up to the emergency. Earlier in 2007, broadcasters provided continuous coverage of Musharraf’s suspension of Chief Justice Chaudhry, helping transform a dispute within the judiciary into a nationwide protest movement led by lawyers and civil-society groups.

Television coverage also brought images of demonstrations and police violence into Pakistani homes. The government temporarily suspended Geo and other channels during earlier confrontations, including unrest in Karachi and the military operation against Islamabad’s Red Mosque.

By November, officials appeared determined to prevent a repeat of the live, round-the-clock coverage that had strengthened the anti-Musharraf movement.

### Pressure ahead of elections

The shutdown occurred as Pakistan prepared for parliamentary elections and as opposition leaders sought to challenge Musharraf’s political allies. Former prime ministers Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif were attempting to return to active politics after years in exile, while lawyers continued protesting the removal of senior judges.

Bhutto initially pursued negotiations with Musharraf over a possible power-sharing arrangement but condemned the emergency and demanded an end to military rule. She was placed under restrictions and briefly prevented from leading political rallies. Sharif, another prominent rival, also called for the restoration of the Constitution and judiciary.

Musharraf later promised elections and said he would relinquish his post as army chief, but opposition groups questioned whether a credible vote could take place while judges were removed, political activists detained and independent news channels silenced.

For many Pakistanis, the disappearance of Geo News and ARY One World became one of the most visible signs of the emergency. Blank screens and entertainment programming replaced live reports from courtrooms, rallies and press conferences.

The government maintained that responsible media outlets would be allowed to operate if they observed official regulations. Journalists countered that the rules required broadcasters to abandon their watchdog role at the precise moment when the country’s political institutions were under the greatest strain.

The conflict underscored a central contradiction of Musharraf’s presidency: private television had flourished after his government liberalized the broadcast sector, but when those channels became powerful forums for criticism, the same administration moved to silence them.
